data.text/markdown:
When a network predicts itself, it gets simpler

A visual essay on Unexpected Benefits of Self-Modeling in Neural Systems by Premakumar et al. (2024, AE Studio and Princeton), arXiv:2407.10188. Neural networks are usually judged by what they get right. This paper asks a stranger question: what happens when a network is also rewarded for predicting its own internal state? The surprise is that it becomes simpler. Adding a self-prediction term to the loss narrows the spread of the final classifier's weights and lowers a formal complexity measure, while test accuracy barely moves. This notebook walks through the idea, our reproduction of Figure 2 on MNIST, and our attempts at the paper's CIFAR-10 (Figure 3) and IMDB (Figure 4) panels. The MNIST panels reproduce. The others only partly do, and the places where they diverge turn out to be the interesting part.

data.text/html: The idea in one picture

data.text/markdown:
The loss

The network keeps its ordinary classification loss. On top of it we add a second job: predict the hidden activations ||(a||) from the same hidden layer, using extra rows of the output layer. ||[L = L_{\mathrm{CE}} + \mathrm{AW} \cdot \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( \hat{a}_i - \mathrm{detach}(a_i) \right)^2||]||(\mathrm{AW}||) is the weight on the self-prediction term and ||(\mathrm{detach}(\cdot)||) is a stop-gradient. The target ||(a||) is detached, so the squared error does not pull on the target copy of ||(a||), only on the prediction ||(\hat{a}||) and the weights that produce it. To see the trade-off, fix an illustrative step with cross-entropy ||(0.35||) and self-prediction MSE ||(0.02||). The slider sets ||(\mathrm{AW}||); the total loss is ||(\mathrm{CE} + \mathrm{AW} \cdot \mathrm{MSE}||).

data.text/markdown:
How we reproduced it

  • Batch size 512. The paper's Table 1 lists 64, which is wrong; we use 512.
  • Detach the target. The self-prediction target is a.detach(), so no gradient flows back through the target copy of the activations.
  • Ten seeds per configuration. Each curve is the mean over 10 seeds, and the bands are the 95% CI half-widths.
  • 120 separate CPU runs. The curves shown come from 120 runs (6 AWs x 10 seeds x 2 preprocessing variants).
  • A batched GPU cross-check. A batched GPU trainer, run independently, agreed with the CPU runs within the 95% CI at every AW.
self_modeling_train.py is that batched trainer, set up for molab's GPU. It reproduces the batched run's epoch-50 means to 5 decimals.

A better ruler: RLCT (Figure 2C)

Weight spread is a crude proxy for complexity. A network can hold many small weights and still have many effective degrees of freedom, and spread says nothing about how the loss actually responds when you move the weights. What we want is a quantity that counts the directions the trained solution is genuinely free to move in. The real log canonical threshold (RLCT), estimated here as the local learning coefficient (LLC), does that. It measures the effective dimensionality of the loss landscape around the trained weights: how fast the loss rises as you wander away from them. We estimate it with a noisy random walk (stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, SGLD) tethered to the trained weights by a localization strength. Lower RLCT means fewer effective parameters, so the same pattern as Figure 2a should show up here as a lower curve for larger self-prediction weights.

At localization 100 our estimates land within about 5% of the paper at every setting where both are well above zero. RLCT rises with hidden size at every AW (at AW = 0 it climbs from 32.5 at hidden 64 to 56.5 at hidden 512), and it falls as AW grows at every size. Both directions point the same way: more self-prediction and smaller networks mean fewer effective parameters. The exceptions are the collapsed settings, where the self-prediction term swamps classification:

  • AW = 50 at hidden 64: -6.0 (95% CI +/- 1.6)
  • AW = 50 at hidden 128: -8.7 (95% CI +/- 11.8)
Negative or near-zero values with wide intervals, matching the paper's own plunge (its hollow points there sit at -4, -5 and -16).

Reproduction note: which localization? The paper's supplement says its MNIST LLC runs used localization 1000, but the caption of its own localization-calibration figure says 100. The choice changes the level. At 1000 our estimates come out up to about 7x lower than the paper's, with the same ordering; at 100 they line up. On pilot models (H=512, AW 0), going from 200 to 4000 draws at localization 1000 moved the estimate only from 8.5 to 8.7. We estimate with a batched SGLD sampler validated against devinterp 2.0.1 (worst relative difference 1.5% on the pilot models). Settings: 4 chains x 4000 draws, nbeta = 82.1 (512/log 512), learning rate 0.0001.

Beyond MNIST: CIFAR-10 (Figure 3)

The paper repeats the experiment on CIFAR-10 with a ResNet-18. The architecture differs from the MNIST MLP: here the classifier reads from a hidden layer of 2000 units, and self-prediction adds output rows that reconstruct that hidden layer. The panels ask the same three questions as before: does weight spread shrink (3A), does RLCT fall (3B), and does accuracy hold (3C)?

Our estimates are flat: 24.8 at AW = 0, 24.0 at AW = 0.5, 24.7 at AW = 1, 24.1 at AW = 2. The spread between the largest and smallest is 0.82, comparable to the individual CIs, so the curves overlap and there is no visible self-modeling effect. The paper reads a monotone fall from 82 to 66, about 20%. Our whole scale also sits roughly 3.0x below the paper's. The same estimator matched the paper on MNIST, so the gap more likely comes from the model or training setup than from the estimator itself.

Accuracy is essentially unchanged by self-modeling: 92.1% to 92.3% across AW, against the paper's 0.918-0.920. The dashed line is the middle of the paper's range. On this panel the reproduction lands, which is what makes the 3A and 3B mismatches worth a second look.

data.text/markdown:
Why does CIFAR go the other way?

Figure 3A and Figure 3B disagree with the paper, but the probes in cifar_fig3_probes.json tell a consistent story: the network is not getting simpler, it is re-parameterizing. The table compares four variants at AW = 0 and AW = 2 (means over two seeds, 50 epochs). hidden |a| is the mean absolute hidden activation on test images; classifier |W| is the L2 norm of the classifier rows. Both are reported first -> last logged epoch.

variant AW SD @ 50 hidden |a| first -> last classifier |W| first -> last
base (detached target) 0 0.0252 0.187 -> 0.209 1.89 -> 3.59
base (detached target) 2 0.0292 0.119 -> 0.191 2.07 -> 4.17
no detach 0 0.0249 0.197 -> 0.210 1.89 -> 3.55
no detach 2 0.0287 0.115 -> 0.158 2.17 -> 4.11
hidden-only target 0 0.0249 0.176 -> 0.215 1.89 -> 3.55
hidden-only target 2 0.0253 0.118 -> 0.180 2.05 -> 3.61
batch 64 0 0.0561 0.078 -> 0.037 2.04 -> 8.07
batch 64 2 0.0765 0.067 -> 0.046 2.22 -> 11.06

What is happening. Under self-modeling the network has a reason to make its hidden activations predictable, and the easiest way is to make them small. In the base run the hidden magnitude at AW = 2 starts at 0.119 versus 0.187 at AW = 0. Smaller activations force larger classifier weights to keep the logits at the same scale, so the weight norm grows further at AW = 2 (4.17) than at AW = 0 (3.59). Weight spread is not scale-invariant: shrink the input and the weights must grow. That is exactly why the paper also reports RLCT, which is invariant to this rescaling. Our RLCT (3B) is flat, so the widening in 3A is a units artifact, not extra complexity. What the probes ruled out.
  • Detach. Removing the stop-gradient (no detach) leaves the inversion in place: SD 0.0249 at AW = 0 and 0.0287 at AW = 2, versus 0.0252 and 0.0292 for base. Gradient flow through the target copy is not the cause.
  • Batch size. Batch 64 changes the level a lot (0.0561 at AW = 0, 0.0765 at AW = 2) but keeps the same ordering, so the inversion is not a batch-size artifact.
  • Hidden-only target. Making the target the hidden layer alone nearly flattens the curves: 0.0249 at AW = 0 and 0.0253 at AW = 2. This is the probe that comes closest to removing the inversion.
What we could not test. The paper describes skip connections from block 3 into the hidden layer. We could not map that onto a standard ResNet-18, so our hidden layer sits after global pooling. That architectural difference is a real candidate for the gap, but we have not isolated it.

IMDB (Figure 4)

The third experiment is sentiment classification on IMDB with an embedding bag and a hidden layer. Figure 4A plots classifier weight SD, 4B is RLCT, and 4C is accuracy. We ran the training panels and estimated 4B's RLCT. The main run is batch 64 with per-model gradient clipping, the setting that matches the paper's batch size; it is plotted by default below.

Bug we found: coupled gradient clipping Our first IMDB runs clipped gradients with one global norm across all stacked models, which coupled otherwise-independent runs and over-clipped each by about ||(\sqrt{M}||). A frozen-head control caught it: AW = 0 lost accuracy even though its self-model term carries zero weight, because the diverging frozen models inflated the shared norm. Clipping is now per-model, and the conclusions did not change. Between the superseded and corrected runs the final SD moved from 0.224 / 0.224 / 0.224 to 0.232 / 0.232 / 0.233, accuracy from 84.9% to 85.2%, and RLCT from 2.399 / 2.427 / 2.427 to 2.100 / 2.125 / 2.127. Every quantity stays flat across AW and far below the paper's scale.

The main run reproduces the paper's accuracy: 85.2% at batch 64, a little above the paper's 0.819-0.836. But no variant separates the AWs. Across the healthy cells the final SD spans at most 0.004, and every curve overlaps every other one. 9 of 150 runs diverged, all of them the no-clip batch-64 variant at AW = 500. The weight SD also sits about 9x below the paper's epoch-500 read-offs: baseline 2.05 in the paper versus 0.232 here. Whatever the paper's self-modeling term does to IMDB, our runs show almost none of it. Hypothesis. Our output layer predicts the hidden activations from those same activations. If the self-model rows can learn to map their input to itself, they can drive the self-model loss to near zero, and then the self-model term stops pushing on the rest of the network. With SGD at learning rate 0.1 and AW up to 500, that shortcut is found quickly. This would explain both failures at once: no AW separation and no movement in the classifier weights. The diagnostics in the next section support this, though on their own they do not prove it.

Figure 4B: RLCT

The RLCT is flat across AW: 2.10, 2.13, and 2.13 (spread 0.03), about 7x below the paper's baseline of 13.7 and nowhere near its 13.7 -> 5.2 slope. This matches the flat weight SD above and is consistent with the identity-map picture supported by the diagnostics below. The estimator follows the paper's supplement settings (devinterp 2.0.1, lr 1e-3, localization 10, nbeta = batch/log(batch) at batch 64, 4 chains x 2000 draws), recorded in imdb_fig4b.json.

Why doesn't IMDB feel the pressure?

The identity-map picture says the self-model term should keep pushing on the network until the self-model rows can predict the hidden activations, at which point the pressure disappears. We logged the self-model loss, the distance of the self-model rows from the identity, and the self-model share of the hidden-layer gradient on shorter diagnostic runs (3 seeds; IMDB 100 epochs, MNIST 50) that mirror the main setups.

data.text/markdown: On IMDB the self-model loss collapses almost immediately, 1.9e-04 at AW 100 and 2.1e-05 at AW 500 by epoch 5, and the self-model share of the hidden-layer gradient falls to 2% and 3% by epoch 20. On MNIST the share is still 14% at AW 10 and 18% at AW 50 at the end of its 50-epoch run. The pressure persists where the effect appears and evaporates where it does not. Why is IMDB so easy? The hidden layer is a linear map of a 64-dimensional embedding, so its 128 activations live in a 64-dimensional subspace; many linear maps reproduce them exactly, and the self-model rows can drive the loss to zero without becoming the identity. They do not: the relative distance ||(\lVert W_s - I\rVert_F / \lVert I\rVert_F||) is still 0.89 at AW 100 and 0.87 at AW 500. The shortcut is a projection, not a copy. We tried to make the test causal by freezing the self-model rows at their random init. Both AW 100 and AW 500 ran away (self-model loss to about 1e+09, accuracy 50%), because a fixed random head with a detached, moving target has no stable solution. That control is therefore inconclusive: it breaks the run rather than holding the shortcut fixed.

Slowing the shortcut down

If the effect is missing on IMDB because the self-model rows learn their shortcut and the pressure dies before it can act, then slowing those rows down should bring it back. We scaled the self-model rows' gradient by 0.01 and 0.001 after per-model clipping and re-ran AW 0/100/500 (3 seeds, 100 epochs); nothing else changed.

At self-model scale 0.01 the pressure survives. The epoch-100 self-model share is 18% at AW 100 and 43% at AW 500, the same range as MNIST. With that pressure still present, AW 100 narrows the epoch-100 SD by -24.6% and AW 500 by -19.1% against the AW 0 baseline; the AW 100 interval does not overlap the baseline and the AW 500 interval does not overlap it. In the normal run (scale 1) the same changes are only -0.1% and +0.1%, and both intervals overlap the baseline. Changing only how fast the shortcut can be learned switches the effect on, which is causal support for the mechanism: the narrowing tracks the pressure, not the run configuration. At self-model scale 0.001 the pressure instead swamps classification. Accuracy falls to 54% and 56%, near the 50% chance line, like the small-network collapse on MNIST, so the classifier never forms and those SDs are not interpretable. The control also has caveats: 3 seeds and 100 epochs; accuracy drops as the self-model rows slow, where the paper's AW 500 is slightly better than baseline; the effect is not monotone in AW (AW 100 narrows more than AW 500); and it is smaller than the paper's. This is a modified setup that explains our null result, not a reproduction of the paper's numbers. Taken with the gradient-share evidence above, the control adds causal evidence for the mechanism, from a small modified experiment: on IMDB the self-model pressure dies before it can act, and when it is held open the classifier narrows as predicted. More seeds and longer runs would firm this up.

The stop-gradient: essential here, irrelevant there

The stop-gradient looks like an implementation detail. It is not. The same ablation does almost nothing on CIFAR and reverses the main MNIST effect. Before you see the numbers: on which dataset does dropping .detach() change the result?

Open questions

  • The CIFAR architecture gap. The paper describes skip connections from block 3 into the hidden layer. We could not map that onto a standard ResNet-18, so our hidden layer sits after global pooling. A faithful implementation is the highest-value next experiment.
  • Is the identity mechanism the whole story? The slow-head control supports it on IMDB, but with 3 seeds, 100 epochs, and a non-monotone effect. More seeds, a longer run, and a scale-invariant read-out would turn a sign into a measurement.
  • Why does the IMDB self-model find a shortcut? The hidden layer is a linear map of a 64-dimensional embedding, so many linear maps reproduce it. A rank diagnostic would say whether the self-model rows learn a projection, as the weight distance suggests.
  • What would falsify the story? A run where the self-model pressure stays high but the weights do not narrow, or one where the weights narrow with the pressure held low.
